theses.title: The one-paragraph story
theses.text:
## The one-paragraph story

Loading rules as prose does not scale: once roughly 140 accumulated feedback
rules ride along, a fresh session starts near 400–500k tokens of always-on
context, where rules fire wrongly or vanish when needed most. In the project's
RPG vocabulary, that is bringing the **whole stash into every map** — as if a character
carried gear for every damage type when the encounter called only for cold
resistance. In plain language, irrelevant rules consumed attention and created
unintended interactions before the task began. The author's implementation
answers with _compiled_ rules: each correction becomes a typed mechanism (a
permission, a guard, a reactor, an evaluator, a transformer, a workflow gate)
attached only where relevant. A session in that profile gets **a build, not a
biography** — one active behavior, a handful of linked supports, its selected
safety layer, and the exact task state. The platform supplies the compiler and
mechanism contracts without prescribing that loadout. The [starter proof](../evidence/WO-118/README.md) completed resident-owned scratch delivery and review repair with writer replacement and resident restart; a fresh export demonstrated live status, while efficiency remains unmeasured.

theses.title: The core bet
theses.text:
## The core bet

> "The true work of the inventor consists in choosing among these combinations
> so as to eliminate the useless ones... the rules that must guide the choice
> are extremely fine and delicate. It's almost impossible to state them
> precisely; they must be felt rather than formulated." — Poincaré, via Pirsig

Generation is cheap and getting cheaper; the scarce asset is the **selection
function** — the operator's sense of what is good, currently exercised one
correction at a time. DotLn's bet is not that this delicate judgment can be
exhaustively formulated. It is that useful operational approximations can be
progressively arrived at: source incidents preserve what was felt, candidate
mechanisms approach it from different directions, and regression fixtures show
where each construction agrees or diverges. As mathematical or geometric
techniques can converge on a shape without becoming the shape itself, the
formulation is an instrument for approaching the operator's selection function,
not a claim to contain it precisely. **The model changes; the organization
survives.** Claude, Codex, a human, a shell script, and a future model are
interchangeable occupants of the same actor slot.

That bet needs an excellent foundation before it needs a long feature list. In
the reference implementation, the smallest useful loop—declare intent, see what
the system understood, observe authorized progress, receive timely feedback,
and inspect evidence—should already feel responsive, legible, and worth
repeating. Competitive gap-filling does not excuse a weak loop. When another
system introduces a useful idea, DotLn first asks whether the exact behavior can
be accommodated by existing primitives, compositions, ports, and runtime
lowerings. If not, the difference becomes evidence for one missing primitive or
boundary, not permission to bolt on an opaque special case. Integration and
semantic accommodation are preferred to imitation; both preserve every
capability contract the receiving implementation declares and expose any
omitted or lossy capability.

theses.title: The differentiated interface
theses.text:
## The differentiated interface

DotLn's second thesis is about _authoring_, not running:

> "I will take the entire Business, Leadership, and Personal Development shelf
> at Barnes & Noble and just map them to different agent / subagent
> communication structures... at once anyone who has read those books is an
> expert in some feature of the app — and it turns all those books into
> programming books overnight."

The analogies are not documentation — **the analogies are the ways you mix and
match the agents**. Every pattern (5S, the Ladder of Leadership, mitigated
speech, Theory of Constraints, commedia dell'arte roles, the
Algorithms-to-Live-By policies) compiles into exact mechanics, and the same
compiled program renders through an open-ended set of isomorphically equivalent
views: an RPG character with a Path-of-Exile-style socket-and-link build, a
business pattern card, a statechart, a function table, a marble/Morse temporal
track, a TypeScript DSL, an event timeline. Friendly metaphors are authoring
languages, never camouflage: every view either provably compiles to the same
normalized program or is labeled a lossy projection with the exact mechanics one
click away.

### Shape-first synthesis

The operator uses situations and analogies to communicate a desired **shape**: a
relationship, interaction, transition, contrast, feedback loop, or felt quality.
Literal similarity to the reference is not the acceptance test unless a specific
literal detail becomes load-bearing. Preserve the experience first, then
progressively lower it through observable interaction, domain mechanics,
contracts and evidence, and finally technology selected from representative
environment evidence. An imperfect analogy can carry a precise requirement;
source accidents do not become ontology by resemblance.

This is the standing interpretation rule for earlier and future operator
ideation. Its fullest product expression is the first-party application thesis,
[`προτείνω`](11-protino.md), but it applies to the whole platform.

theses.title: Three horizons, one kernel
theses.text:
## Three horizons, one kernel

1. **Work operating system** — workstreams, disposable workers, evidence-backed
   completion, offline-capable state, a near-empty main thread. The immediate
   product.
2. **Executable pattern workshop** — the shelf-to-mechanism compiler and the
   drag-a-card-onto-an-agent authoring surface. The differentiated product.
3. **Agent ecology & simulation laboratory** — paired counterfactual runs,
   first-divergence detection, agent swaps, reflection-policy experiments over
   recorded event logs. The research product.

Horizon 3 must emerge from the same kernel (deterministic replay is what makes
counterfactuals possible at all) and is not allowed to distort Horizon 1.
The [workstream application candidate](12-workstream-application.md) develops
Horizon 1 through concrete end-user journeys and gradual workflow replacement,
including one outcome spanning multiple repositories. It leaves deployment and
application identity open and does not allocate another release rung.
[`προτείνω`](11-protino.md) is the operator-named application destination that
joins Horizons 2 and 3: prose-authored patterns and ad hoc interventions become
playable inside an inspectable counterfactual community. Naming the destination
does not move it ahead of the release ladder or make its application-local
content kernel doctrine.

theses.title: Mission — increase the chance of operator flow
theses.text:
## Mission — increase the chance of operator flow

This is the mission of the author's personal implementation and a motivating
use of the platform, not a compulsory objective or operating policy for every
DotLn owner.

AI-assisted work commonly falls into a babysitting mode: the operator repeatedly
restates context, supplies procedural guidance, coordinates tools and workers,
checks unsupported completion claims, recovers stalled work, and spends active
attention on the machinery instead of the idea. The desired alternative is not
unbounded improvisation or confidence without evidence. It is a sustained
creative flow in which the operator can keep the idea and implementation
direction in mind while the surrounding work behaves dependably.

The reference implementation's mission is to improve the conditions for that
**operator flow state**.
Supporting research, capability-building, coordination, routine procedure,
recovery, and verification should happen automatically when authorized,
predictably when routine, and helpfully when a genuinely material decision needs
the operator. Product and research investment should favor capabilities that
remove recurring supervision and avoidable context switches without exporting
their cost into correctness, authority, evidence, privacy, or recoverability.

The implementation cannot promise or infer a person's psychological state. It can
reduce interruption, repetition, manual ceremony, and rediscovery; preserve
intent and working context across handoffs; package necessary interruptions as
decision-ready inputs; and make recovery unsurprising. Under its selected
profile, flow does not silently authorize scope expansion, skipped verification,
perpetual action, or self-certification. “Give an agent a build, not your
biography” remains useful architectural shorthand for one mechanism serving
this larger mission.

exclusions.text:
Not an agent, an agent harness, or an agent-orchestration layer, as its
  identity. DotLn is an **agentic platform**: the shared substrate on which
  people and software actors hold work, authority, and evidence. It contains an
  orchestration layer and hosts harnesses as observed environments
  ([runtime primitive catalogs](03-architecture.md#runtime-primitive-catalogs)),
  but neither of those is what it is.
Not a prompt library, and not a wrapper that makes one vendor's model nicer.

Not a prescribed catalog of ideal agents, roles, personalities, workflows, or
  organizational doctrine. Bundled patterns are examples and optional starting
  points, not kernel truth.

Not dependent on a public marketplace. Local files, private catalogs,
  organization-internal registries, and offline or air-gapped installations
  remain complete authoring and distribution paths.

Not one prescribed autonomy curve. Presence and recorded time are policy
  inputs; an explicit owner policy may hold, shrink, grow, peak, reset, or loop
  scope and authority within its declared ceiling.

In the reference implementation, not a metrics theater: no invented numbers,
  no activity-as-progress, evidence precedes "done," and utilization is not the
  objective. A profile that omits verification says so instead.

The reference implementation is not finished when it works for its author:
  v1.0 means a person who has never read these docs can declare a bounded intent
  and receive a verifiable result.

An `extensions` section with a root under a kit tree, a symlinked root,
   an uncontained module, a duplicate id, an unknown kind, or an adapter
   whose `suite` names no declared suite or a suite whose `sources` omit
   its module refuses naming the key, and an absent section loads as the
   default root with no adapters; a `suites` entry with a duplicate or
   non-lowercase name, an empty or non-string `command` or an uncontained
   source refuses naming the key, and an absent section loads as none; a
   `build.channel` outside the three, or a malformed `build.pin`, refuses
   naming the key, and an absent channel reads as `both` (configuration
   cases).

The fixture vertical runs from intake to contract with an issue naming
   `source: "fixture"`: the adapter's bundle passes
   `requireCompleteIssueBundle`, the screen and `decodeSourceBundle` as the
   GitHub source's does, and the record the decisions name holds
   `ExtensionLoaded` with the module's SHA-256; an undeclared id refuses at
   configuration; a wrong export shape refuses naming the id (vertical and
   extension cases).

Declared `effect` and `projection` adapters are listed by kind with
   their contained paths and SHA-256 and never imported (their top-level
   markers stay absent after listing and after a vertical run); no consumer
   runs them (extension cases).

An export from a core checkout carries no path under the extension root
   and the manifest lists none; in a fixture instance an update leaves the
   root byte-identical and refuses a planted kit path inside it (launchpad
   cases).

The kit manifest (schema 2) names its build files as the relative-import
   closure of `contributor.js` and `feedback.js` inside
   `packages/skeleton/dist/src/loadouts/` (six files at `926b8234`), its
   semantic hash and compiler package version; a schema 1 manifest reads as
   all machinery (fixture).

Under `machinery` an update replaces every kit file but the build
   modules, which keep their pinned bytes, records `build.pin` and leaves
   the emitted bundle at the pinned build after the re-emit; under `build`
   only the build modules change and the re-emit produces the new build
   over unchanged machinery; under `both` the plan equals today's; the
   preview shows the partition and the channel in each case (fixture).

The from-core preview and the update's summary label and count
   byte-identical replace rows `unchanged`, with `planUpdate`'s kinds, the
   writes and the receipt unchanged; the in-instance revision preview lists
   an absent manifest-listed kit path the incoming manifest still carries as
   a local-removal row (unchanged upstream when its incoming and prior
   hashes match), prints every other row and declared action and exits 0,
   while the from-core preview and the update still refuse it before any
   write (fixture).

A `machinery` update whose incoming compiler is incompatible with the
   pin, and a `build` update whose definitions are incompatible with the
   installed compiler, refuse before any write and print the two choices;
   compatibility is the Design's guard (the major from 1.0, the minor below
   it, every imported name present in the pinned modules, every name a pinned
   module imports still exported by the machinery module outside `build.files`
   that it imports); a channel or pin
   beside an overlay's `build: "none"` refuses before any emit or update
   write (fixture).

`harness emit` from a pinned build produces the pinned revision's
   bundle; `harness check` passes with the pin and refuses a pinned module
   whose bytes differ (fixture).

In a fixture instance that merged a starter revision, `build --pin`
    restores and verifies the pinned modules from its history,
    `build --take` adopts the merged modules and moves the pin, each prints
    the re-emit instruction, and both refuse when the history lacks the

    `packages/<name>/dist/` file (fixture).

An overlay composed over a pinned build equals its composition at the

    channel, the plan, the applied actions) and retains a copy of each file

    so a release close after this order refreshes the starter without a

A rollback after an update restores every kit file to the prior

In an exported instance, `request draft` writes a typed draft in the
   ignored lane and leaves no tracked change in `git status`; the kit manifest lists the command, its templates and the
   deployment-record template, and none of the drafts lane or ledger.

`request check` reports each screen's result on fixture drafts: one
   clean; one with a term from a synthetic local-terms list; one with an
   off-host address; one with no terms list, reported as unavailable and
   treated as not passed.

`request ready` sets a draft's `ready` with the operator's word as given
   and refuses an empty word; neither the ledger nor the filed issue
   carries the word. `request file` refuses, with a typed reason naming the
   cause, a draft whose `ready` is null, a draft with a failing or unavailable screen, any
   draft while `requests.route` is `none`, and a `direct` filing when the
   `UPSTREAM.md` block names no repository; under `manual` it prints the
   title and body and makes no network call, shown by a fixture that fails
   on any spawned forge command; under `manual`, `request file <id> --reference <issue>` records the
   reported reference in the ledger without a network call and a later
   answered list marks the row delivered; under `direct` a fixture forge command
   receives exactly the title, body and label and the ledger records the
   returned reference.

`npm run plan -- requests` over a fixture forge listing writes one
   register candidate per labelled open issue with its reference and bundle
   hash, nothing for an issue already registered, and the reader's typed
   stop for an issue whose bundle is incomplete; `plan start` returns the
   count of requests not yet disposed.

`parseHeader` reads the `dotln-requests` block; the index card prints
   it; the pull-request body published for an order naming a request
   carries that request's closing reference, and `worktree publish`
   refuses a body that lacks it unless the request's ledger row records a
    disposition other than this order's (declined, superseded or answered
    elsewhere), which the body then names; an order naming no request is
    unchanged.

A from-core update fixture from a recorded core commit to a later one
   prints, in the instance-actions note, the requests answered by the
   releases between them; the sibling receipt lists the same issue numbers
   and the ledger marks them delivered with the version. A starter-merge
   preview fixture prints the same requests and writes no receipt, and the
   next `request` run after the merge marks the ledger the same way.

The kit carries the deployment-record template; the instance's
   pre-drafted first order names filling it; `requests.route` is documented
   there with its default.

One live request: from a scratch export with `requests.route` set to
    `direct` under the operator's grant, one generic request, drafted by
    the executor from the operator's guidance and marked ready on the
    operator's recorded word, is filed to this repository, read by
    `plan -- requests` and registered; its evidence records the issue
    reference, the bundle hash and the register row, and no text beyond
    the request itself.

The write-backs of step 11 state: in 03, the request route as
    implemented for issues; in 07, `plan -- requests` among the entry
    reads; in 12, the route and its floor beside the request row (the parity-map
    sentences left product 12 on 2026-10-30 with the retired WO-228); in 07, that the pasted-block route of its planning-pass
    item 5 ends when this order lands; in the client README, the command. The decisions file
    and index; the publication locks refreshed.

The re-mints of step 9 are recorded; `npm test -- --review` and
    `npm run test:docs` green; `git diff --check` clean; no new dependency.
    No live feedback episode is owed.

Phase 1: reconcile the runbook's recorded posture, the startup
evidence and the ADR claims for each harness the runbook records with a
qualified role (Claude Code, Codex CLI and Copilot CLI) at recorded versions,
as dated observations with a drift rule, with settings readback treated as
configuration evidence and never as proof of reduced approval burden. Phases 2
and 3, the planning map's boarded candidate, would make approval behavior an
observable, executable acceptance contract measured by the prompts actually
encountered in fresh sessions and reduce unnecessary boundary crossings by
fixing scripts, paths and invocation structure, never by disabling a sandbox,
enabling unsandboxed fallback or adding a broad or persistent allow rule; they
reopen when a host channel reports approval requests.

2026-09-01 and filed at `039788a7`):**

  September 1 sandboxed configuration is kept as a reference, and Claude's
  mode is operator-attested, not probed. Several criteria as filed
  presume an enabled host sandbox: scenario C's "documented sandbox";
  criterion 11's denials, where with no filesystem sandbox command rules

  runner refuses because its skeleton and portfolio suites need the
  outside. Under Codex approval `never` no approval request is raised, so

  posture is not decided here.

  classifying interruptions: no approval-surface matrix exists under

## Goal-aligned decisions

The Contributor's purpose comes from [the vision](00-vision.md): DotLn is a
local-first, model-agnostic compiler/runtime for human judgment. This personal
implementation aims to improve operator flow by moving recurring supervision,
coordination, recovery and verification into dependable machinery, while
preserving correctness, authority, evidence, privacy and recoverability.

The current [critical-path plan](../planning/critical-path-2026-09-08.md) targets
the always-on runtime, its first real external source change and an independently
verified source-to-deliverable loop.

<!-- dotln-goal-rules:start -->

The [sequence](../planning/sequence.md) and selected work order determine
current placement and authority. The mission is the outcome; the critical path
is the dependency route to the next outcome. Useful prerequisite or
risk-reduction work must name the blocked outcome it enables. Process activity,
receipt volume and agent utilization are not progress by themselves. Goal
alignment grants no authority to reorder or expand work. In all phases, the Goal
Alignment and Process Cost procedure lives in the generated role skills
[WO-043, 2026-09-11].

Accuracy takes priority over agreement in every phase. The already-equipped
Correctness over Sycophancy rule applies to operator suggestions and the agent's
own premises equally: challenge unsupported claims, distinguish observation
from inference, state material uncertainty, and correct mistakes when evidence
changes. A confident request or an earlier decision is not proof of correctness.
Record material disagreement and its evidence in the same decision or phase
receipt; do not manufacture dissent or seek approval for ordinary judgment.

| Lens                                  | Decision question                                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Policy resistance / fixes that fail   | Will local goals or guards undo one another?                                                              |
| Tragedy of the commons                | Does the solution consume shared compute, context or operator attention without accounting for the total? |
| Drift to low performance              | Does it improve an explicit outcome standard rather than normalize a worse baseline?                      |
| Escalation                            | Will additional process provoke more process or workarounds?                                              |
| Success to the successful             | Are credible alternatives excluded merely because the current mechanism already has investment?           |
| Shifting the burden to the intervenor | Does the solution remove recurring operator rescue or depend on it?                                       |
| Rule beating                          | Can the evidence pass without the intended behavior occurring?                                            |
| Seeking the wrong goal                | Does it advance operator flow and the selected product outcome rather than a proxy?                       |

Naive Interventionism adds the existing system's useful functions, affected
consumers, second-order harm, reversibility and smallest useful probe. NoOp
records what happens if nothing changes, why action or inaction wins, and the
evidence that would reopen the choice. Scale detail to consequence: explain
applicable risks and briefly group immaterial lenses with a reason; do not
manufacture eight repetitive paragraphs for routine edits.

Record evidence of benefit and the risks of intervening in existing behavior;
verification and handoff compare observed outcomes with the promised benefit.
Required legal or release actions retain their existing authority; NoOp is a
considered alternative, not an ambient veto or permission to abandon authorized
work.

<!-- dotln-goal-rules:end -->

**Platform lens.** Four checks from the platforms lesson the operator
pointed at (Steve Yegge's 2011 account of the Amazon service mandate) apply
to any capability a plan or order lands: it arrives as an interface
something else consumes (a transport profile, a typed event, a projection, a
handoff packet), never only as a script or a session; it is externalizable
by construction (content-addressed inputs, declared contracts, no private
setting as the source of a guarantee); this repository and the operator's
own repository consume it before any export; and its result is usable by a
stranger to the session, so a receipt that needs reverse-engineering is an
accessibility failure [[vision-into-use pass](../planning/vision-into-use-2026-09-17.md)
§12, 2026-09-17]. The planning refuter's platform-first standard is
unchanged.

<!-- dotln-goal-rules:start -->

Material choices and rationales go in existing phase evidence: per-order
`docs/evidence/WO-NNN/decisions.md` and cited product sections for work-order
decisions; planning dispositions/candidate records for planning choices; the
independent report or refutation receipt for its judgment; retained closeout
evidence for release decisions. The decisions index exposes per-order records.
Reuse and link a current rationale until its assumptions change; do not create
a parallel decision log or an extra approval ritual.

<!-- dotln-goal-rules:end -->

The shared supports carry these duties and their compiled identity in both
harnesses. They are instruction-level judgment, not proof that an agent applied
every lens or a causal detector. The meter's five quantitative trap signals are
separate. General Naive Interventionism, NoOp and adaptive Tinkerer mechanics
retain their candidate scope; this bounded Contributor policy does not claim
their generalized implementations. The [WO-043 receipt](../evidence/WO-043/ideation-commands-and-usage.md)
records this promotion and its limits.

episode.statement: Plan refuter (Entropy Reducer identity, Contra-Auguste mask, architecture-and-semantics lens) for planning pass planning-2026-10-30-b. I read <worktree>/docs/control/local/planning-2026-10-30-b/refute-prompt-2.txt: its four header lines, and its fifth line parsed with node as one JSON document with the keys identity, mask, lens, role, workOrder, subject, outputInstructions, resultSchema and workerInstructions. In subject I read standard (theses, exclusions, roles, rolesTable, capabilities), goalReview (platformStandard, goalStandard, criticalPath, evidenceHash, observations, costEvidenceStatus), orders for WO-240, WO-237, WO-241, WO-242, WO-243, WO-244, WO-207 and WO-193 (title, objective, cost, criteria, nonGoals), scope, sequence, deferrals and costTable (rows, traps, acceptances, firstVerifications). I also ran git rev-parse --show-toplevel and wc on that file, and validated the result against resultSchema in memory with node; one validation probe passed its input through a shell here-document, which the shell may back with a transient temporary file it removes itself. I read no other repository file, no planner narrative and no previous receipt; host-supplied session instructions were present in context, and the judgment rests on the compiled subject. Result: plan verdict aligned-with-findings with no holds; all eight orders aligned-with-findings, each with known issues and concrete reopening observations. I wrote no files, made no repository or Git writes, ran no gate and spawned no agent.

orders.criticalPathAndNoOp: Gate: none directly. WO-192 sits in no row of the supplied critical-path table and no gate's blocking prerequisites name it. The nearest gate is P (WO-080 -> WO-081, WO-082 -> WO-083, the fork's run); the sequence places WO-192 immediately before WO-083 so that run is driven by the router, but WO-083's committed dependency block (docs/work-orders/WO-083-real-run-launchpad-instance.md) lists WO-118, WO-080, WO-072, WO-201, WO-202, WO-210, WO-213 and WO-204 as hard and WO-073, WO-078 as satisfied-by-close, never WO-192, and its title drives the order 'the way core drives orders at that time'. So WO-192 unblocks no gate: it is mission work (Horizon 1's disposable workers and near-empty main thread; the mission's removal of manual ceremony and handoffs) that changes how gate P's run is driven, not whether it can run. NoOp in the records: the operator keeps typing one phrase per phase in separate sessions, at least four per first-pass order plus one per repair. The Cost line files 6.25 implied operator phrases per order over the record (6.94 since 2026-10-08), a hand-gap share of 30.5% of within-order wall clock (33.2% since 2026-10-08) and a 3.6-minute median wait from implementation-ready to verification requested (17.8 since 2026-10-08), from 165 control segments at 49d8c4c3; I confirmed 49d8c4c3 is an ancestor of acd1c94f but did not recompute the figures, whose method sits in the planning narrative this refutation may not read. Under NoOp WO-083 runs on hand-typed phrases, which its own text admits. The NoOp cost is operator attention and hand-gap wall clock, not a blocked outcome; action wins on the mission thesis provided the benefit is measured (finding on criterion 9), and the observation that would reopen the choice is the first driven orders' segments failing to lower those figures.
orders.systemTraps: Policy resistance: the order adds one refusal kind (router spawns whose prompt is not exactly a lifecycle phrase) beside the observed guard-refusal series 2, 10, 0, 0, 8, and two of its own rules can undo each other: the per-agent writer key against pid-based owner liveness (harness-host.ts resolves a Claude owner from CLAUDE_PID, which in-process workers share), so an interrupted worker's reservation blocks the re-dispatch criterion 8 promises; and the phrase-only spawn rule against operator directions written on resume phrases. Tragedy of the commons: the driven-session ceiling (default four times subagentCap, 80) equals four separate phase sessions' allowance, so spawn count is at parity; tokens and dollars stay null under the WO-126 policy (docs/control/budgets.json dispatches carry tokens and costUsd null), the main thread's share relocates into workers rather than disappearing (the Cost line's own words), and every session, driven or not, pays step 3's CLAUDE.md line and step 6's fan-out sentence. Drift to low performance: the observation records executor 29,484 over 29,246 and reviewer 29,584 over 28,884, both breach, and the order deepens both with only a before/after byte record (finding on criterion 12). Escalation: probe-first plus a named fallback bounds the mechanism, but the in-process branch alone adds identity rekeying, per-spawner counters, a grant kind and a refusal the fallback does not need, and a second lifecycle driver for target orders beside the resident's runtime actors invites later reconciliation when both read one order. Success to the successful: the resident coordinator and router-reads-reports alternatives are declined with stated reasons, not by investment alone; choosing the harness hook path over the latent runtime.work-order-transport row is defensible for a Contributor-only role. Shifting the burden to the intervenor: the order removes the recurring hand handoff, the mission's core target, yet routes back to the operator at every stop, and the supplied observation shows corrections in four of the last five orders and 52 lifecycle directions on WO-219, each of which becomes a stop under drive. Rule beating: criterion 9 can pass with parent-session hooks governing a target worker, which the Design excludes; criterion 4's fail-before anchor is the 2026-10-02 commit 08845c71 rather than the activation base, harmless only because no router exists in between (none at acd1c94f). Seeking the wrong goal: the criteria verify mechanism (one phrase typed in a fixture drive with synthetic gate commands) while the outcome (fewer phrases, smaller hand-gap, shorter waits) is filed as before-numbers with no after-measure; the observed machinery share (0.20 to 0.31 of elapsed time, not worsening) raises no current alarm, and this order's own process cost (executor max, a live drive, the review gate) is of the size that signal watches.
orders.removalBalance: Partly. On the operator-attention axis, the mission's axis, the named removal exceeds the addition: at least four typed phrases and hand-carried handoffs per first-pass order (more per repair) become one phrase per drive and one after the merge, against one new phrase to learn, and the four existing phrases stay, so nothing is taken from an operator who prefers separate sessions. On the machinery and context axes the order is net additive and its Cost line says so: a router role and root, four generated agent definitions, session, role and writer rekeying by agent, per-spawner counting with a new driven-session ceiling, a new refusal, a new grant kind, a route reading, new budget keys, a probe mode, a role-oracle fixture, target-order text in three roots and bytes added to every root. No hook, rule, file or byte is removed; the single worker definition stays; the main thread's share of phase work is relocated, not removed; and the launchpad npm test dropped from target-order role text is replaced by the target gate, a substitution rather than a removal. Two corrections to scale: the plural agent-definition generator the Cost line attributes to this order already exists at acd1c94f (packages/compiler/src/harness.ts declares workers? at line 283 and loops it at line 1006; contributor.ts declares workers at line 888; .claude/agents holds dotln-worker.md and dotln-worker-fable.md; landed in af73b1fb on 2026-10-22), so the addition is smaller than stated; and if the probe selects the separate-session fallback, the identity, counter and refusal additions may have no consumer (finding on criterion 1). Wall clock, tokens and context bytes are honestly marked unknown until run; unknown cost is not a structural hold.
orders.failureBehavior: Mostly degrades to the old behavior. A failed probe row selects the named fallback (each phase a separate root session through the existing print transport, needing no identity or counter change); the router never merges and stops with a one-line next step at a merge, a routed finding, an off-ramp or correction, analysis: or operator override:, a refused dispatch, the repair bounds, two unrecorded completions and an exhausted budget; the four existing phrases keep their behavior, so every stop falls back to today's per-phase operation; the spawn refusal applies only to the router role and never to a worker's own spawns, so non-driven sessions are untouched; an unattributable spawn is counted as a stated minimum as today, and the existing counter admits with an advisory when the cap is unavailable (packages/skeleton/src/subagent-budget.ts); readBudgets reading an absent router entry as null keeps earlier exports' npm run meta working, where readBudgets otherwise throws for a missing dispatch kind (scripts/lib/process-budget.mjs); the merged read without fetch fails safe toward not-merged; Codex and Copilot fall back to role text and advice. Two places refuse rather than degrade: an in-process worker that ends without recording completion keeps a writer reservation whose owner pid (the shared host process) stays alive, so the re-dispatched worker is refused and recovery needs the router's recorded observation, which no criterion fixtures, or an operator-terminal writer --release --force under operator override; and a direction written on a phrase cannot reach a worker under the phrase-only rule, which ends the drive in a stop, safe but with the drive's benefit lost for that order.

The Cost line grows both roots (step 3's CLAUDE.md line, step 6's fan-out sentence, step 9's target-order text) and criterion 12 only has the decisions record bytes before and after; it names neither an acceptance under the standing 2026-09-17 route, which the recorded acceptances say never leaves a breach advisory across orders, nor a byte removal. Not a hold: the breach predates this order, the budget is advisory (requireBudgets in scripts/lib/process-budget.mjs only warns) and the standing route answers it; the repair is one clause in criterion 12 requiring a dated acceptance or a removal for every root the order leaves above its ceiling.

findings.reason: Writer liveness is judged by host process: harness-host.ts resolves a Claude owner from CLAUDE_PID and ownerDead calls harnessProcessAlive on that pid. In-process workers share the router's host process, so once the reservation is keyed by session and agent, a worker that ends without recording completion leaves a reservation whose owner stays alive and is never reclaimed as dead. The Design releases it by the router's recorded observation that the worker ended, but criterion 5 fixtures only release by recorded completion and criterion 8's re-dispatch case is a status table test, so nothing shows the fresh re-dispatched worker can write; the path then refuses (the writer refusal points to writer --release --force from an operator terminal) instead of degrading.
findings.reopenWhen: A fixture or driven run in which a worker ends without recording completion and the re-dispatched worker's first write is refused by the ended worker's reservation, or criterion 5's fixtures land without a router-observed-end release case.

findings.reason: The in-process design rests on each worker's working directory being the order's worktree (criterion 4 forbids carrying the order in the prompt; the router runs in the main checkout), yet the behaviors named under Probe first include no row for whether the spawning call can set a worker's working directory at all. WO-139's recorded spawn inputs at Claude 2.1.276 (docs/evidence/WO-139/subagent-probe-2.json) carry only description, prompt, subagent_type and run_in_background, and the Agent spawn schema visible in this refuter's own session exposes no working-directory field (an inference from that schema; its host version is unknown to me). If no such control exists, the in-process form cannot meet criterion 9's working-directory record and the separate-session fallback applies, leaving criteria 4 to 6 (router spawn refusal, per-agent identity, per-spawner budget) as machinery the selected design may not use; criterion 1 says later criteria are met in that design without naming which ones the fallback discharges.

Drift to low performance: no role root or cold-start byte change, so the worsening coldStartBytes series is not fed by this order. orders.removalBalance: No. The Cost line names as its removal three states (only the operator’s runtime ever gated; no comparison of the running Node with engines; a misleading npm ci warning on Node 24 hosts), none measured. The addition is concrete: engines edits in seven package files and the lockfile, a refusing host check with fixtures, one complete gate run of about 25 to 33 minutes, README passages and re-mints, and a permanent second supported line that every later machinery change must keep compatible without any recurring Node 24 run. The removal is a risk reduction for adopters the records do not count; it is not larger than the addition in recorded cost.
orders.failureBehavior: It refuses rather than degrading, by design. checkHost refuses an out-of-range or unparsable version at the first gate task; before the order such a host received an npm ci warning and the gate ran. A host whose runtime leaves the range (a Node 27 upgrade; a 26.x prerelease, by inference refused under the same semver rule that refuses v24.15.0-rc.1; or an older line an instance ran under the warning) loses its gate entirely, and the judged fields name no override or degraded mode. Inside the range behavior equals the old one apart from the comparison; the engines field itself still only warns at npm ci.

Inference: if the reuse key carries no runtime, whichever run comes second at one identity can be satisfied by rows produced under the other runtime, so the Node 24 record can pass without the suites running on Node 24.
